feedback: Accept a counterexample only if the learner explains why that multiplier shrinks (it is less than 1 / a part of the quantity).
If the corrected rule says 'fractions make it smaller', challenge with 5/3 × 7 and ask them to refine the rule to 'less than 1'.
activities.intendedInsight: Refuting the over-generalised belief requires producing a counterexample and restating the condition precisely, which strengthens understanding of why the threshold is 1.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'multiplying a number always makes it bigger.'
Find a specific case that shows the claim is false and explain why it fails (e.g. 3/4 × 7 is three-quarters OF 7, so less than 7).
Then state the corrected, precise rule: multiplying a positive quantity makes it bigger only when the multiplier is greater than 1; by 1 it stays the same; by less than 1 it gets smaller.
Explain why 5/3 × 7 does make 7 bigger, so the rule is about size relative to 1, not about being a fraction.
activities.title: Find the counterexample to 'multiplying always makes bigger'

feedback: If a learner says 7 × 4/4 is bigger or smaller 'because you multiplied', point out that 4/4 = 1 and that ×1 leaves the quantity unchanged.
Have the learner show the bar holding its length while the partition changes, linking equal length to equal value.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1: it rescales the name (re-partitions) without changing the value, which is exactly what underlies equivalent fractions.
learnerActions: Predict what 7 × 4/4 equals and whether it is bigger, smaller, or the same as 7.
Show on a bar or number line that 4/4 is one whole, so the length holds while being re-partitioned into quarters.
Connect this to fraction equivalence: multiplying a/b by n/n (n a whole number greater than 1) gives a different name for the same value.
Explain why 3/4 × 2/2 names the same value as 3/4.
activities.title: Multiplying by n/n keeps the value
